title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.7166 – Reuters estimate
body: The People's Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day's closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point.

title: ICYMI: US begins returning staff to Middle East embassies after Iran war evacuations
body: The gradual return of diplomatic staff is a meaningful, if incremental, signal that Washington now assesses near term escalation risk with Iran as lower, even though the underlying conflict remains formally unresolved, with the naval blockade of Iran and closure of the Strait of Hormuz both still in place. This sits alongside the broader de-escalatory signals already seen this week, the Rubio comments on shifting from strikes to sanctions, and the unconfirmed ceasefire report, adding another data point supporting the view that active combat operations are unlikely to resume in the near term. For oil markets already pricing in reduced geopolitical risk, this reinforces rather than reverses the recent trend, though the partial nature of the staffing restoration, several posts capped well below full capacity, signals Washington is not yet treating the region as fully stabilised. -- Washington isn't declaring the Iran crisis over, but it's stopped acting like it could get worse any minute.

title: Hawkish board member Tamura to represent BOJ at Jackson Hole instead of Ueda
body: Ueda's decision to skip Jackson Hole removes one of the more direct opportunities for the BOJ governor to signal policy intent on the world stage this week, shifting attention instead to whether he attends the G20 finance ministers and central bank governors meeting in Asheville, North Carolina, running 31 August to 1 September. With markets already near fully pricing a September BOJ hike following the joint US-Japan yen intervention and a nudge from Treasury Secretary Bessent, any sidelines interaction between Ueda and Bessent at that G20 gathering could carry outsized signalling value for yen crosses. In the interim, Thursday's speech and press conference from Deputy Governor Himino becomes the more immediate catalyst, while sending a known hawk in Tamura to Jackson Hole in Ueda's place is itself a modest signal given the currently near- consensus view among economists that the BOJ moves to 1.25% at its 17-18 September meeting. --- Ueda is skipping the world's most-watched central banking conference just as the world starts fully pricing his next move.

title: Palm Oil Retreats to One-Week Low
body: Malaysian palm oil futures extended their decline, slipping below MYR 4,900 per tonne and hitting a one‑week low as traders returned from the holiday break. Market sentiment came under pressure from a stronger ringgit and weaker soyoil prices on the Chicago Board of Trade, while crude oil retreated on renewed optimism that the Strait of Hormuz could reopen. Demand worries further weighed on prices. Cargo surveyor Intertek Testing Services reported that exports of palm oil products for August 1–25 fell 20% compared with the same period in July. Ample supply added to the bearish tone, with Malaysian palm oil inventories rising to a five‑month high in July. In addition, exports from top producer Indonesia dropped 9.2% year-on-year in June, according to the industry group GAPKI. Losses were partially limited by stronger soyoil prices on the Dalian exchange. Concerns that a developing El Niño could intensify dryness and curb output in Indonesia and Malaysia also lent support, as did Indonesia's plan to fully implement its B50 biodiesel mandate from October 1. title: Wheat Futures Hit 1-Month High
body: Wheat futures approached $7 per bushel in late August, their highest level since July 23, as escalating hostilities between Russia and Ukraine threatened further disruption to Black Sea grain exports. The deepening conflict has heightened concerns about the capacity of these two key wheat exporters to ship their crops to global markets, just as the new harvest accelerates. According to the US Department of Agriculture, Russia is expected to export 46 million metric tons of wheat in the current marketing year, while Ukraine's exports are projected at 13.5 million tons. Adding to the upward pressure on prices, US wheat export inspections declined to 425,668 metric tons in the week ended August 20, down from 514,363 tons the previous week and sharply below the 1.05 million tons inspected in the same week a year earlier. At the same time, the US spring wheat harvest continued to advance rapidly, with 62% of the crop harvested as of Sunday, up from 41% a week earlier and exceeding the five-year average of 52%. title: Soybeans Hold at 1-Month High
body: Soybean futures remained above $12.20 per bushel, hovering near a four-week high, as deteriorating US crop conditions and renewed export demand lent support to prices. The USDA's national soybean rating declined over the past week, with the share of the crop rated good-to-excellent slipping 1 percentage point to 60% for the week ended August 23. While 91% of the crop has reached the pod-setting stage, traders are closely monitoring whether further deterioration could curb production potential and tighten the balance sheet ahead of harvest. At the same time, private exporters reported the sale of 132,000 tonnes of new-crop US soybeans to an unknown destination, prompting market speculation that China may be the buyer. The prospective purchase comes as US–China trade tensions remain in focus, with the possibility of new US tariffs on Chinese goods adding uncertainty to the outlook for soybean demand. Markets are also watching a potential late-September meeting between Trump and Xi, which could prove pivotal for future agricultural trade flows. title: Copper Hits Fresh Record High
body: Copper futures rose above $6.70 per pound on Wednesday, setting a new record high as supply risks remained elevated despite a recent easing of the market squeeze. Traders continued to redirect shipments to the United States, drawn by strong premiums and the prospect of new tariffs under a potential Trump administration, although the White House has not yet reached a final decision. Stockpiles in London Metal Exchange–monitored warehouses have declined by nearly 50% since mid-May, following a 42-day stretch of continuous drawdowns. At the same time, Zijin Mining warned that flooding at the Kamoa-Kakula copper complex in the Democratic Republic of Congo could reduce its share of output by up to 57,000 tons this year, highlighting persistent threats to global supply. On the demand side, Chinese smelters have struggled to secure sufficient feedstock, further bolstering the need for imported copper. title: Corn Hits 3-Year High on US Crop Concerns
body: Corn futures climbed above $5 per bushel, reaching their highest level since July 2023, as growing worries over US crop yields signaled tighter supplies ahead. The Pro Farmer Crop Tour recently pegged the 2026 US corn yield at 173.2 bushels per acre, significantly below the USDA's latest estimate of 180.7 bushels per acre, with total production projected at 15.34 billion bushels. The increasingly bearish supply outlook was underscored by the USDA's most recent crop report, which showed the share of corn rated good-to-excellent falling three percentage points to 57% for the week ended August 23. Weather conditions remain a critical factor, as heat stress and excessive rainfall across parts of the Midwest threaten to curb yields as harvest approaches. At the same time, US corn export inspections remain robust. Cumulative shipments are up 26% from a year earlier, even though weekly volumes have recently eased to 1.3 million tonnes. On the global front, ongoing disruptions to Black Sea grain shipments continue to fuel concerns about worldwide supply availability.
